label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
Peter, I want to push back on this one, and I want to do it respectfully, because your payroll experience is exactly why your concerns are worth taking seriously. You’re right that an informal, unlimited advance scheme is a bad idea. You’re right that it can teach people to live on next month’s money. You’re right that recovery from leavers is a real risk, and you’re right that HR should not be running a cash window from an office. I don’t disagree with any of that.

Where I think the conclusion goes wrong is the step from “informal advances are bad” to “therefore close the window.” We tried that. I’m HR manager at a logistics business of about 340 staff, with depots in Embakasi and Changamwe — mostly drivers, turn-boys, loaders and warehouse clerks. In February 2025, after exactly the same pushback from Finance, we closed our advance scheme. The argument was almost word for word what you’ve written: we’re not a bank, SACCOs exist, give notice, do financial literacy, people will adjust. We gave two months’ notice and ran one financial literacy session with our SACCO. Then we closed it.

By August, reception had logged 61 calls from debt collectors and loan apps. Before that it was a handful. Some of the apps were calling supervisors whose names had been put down as referees. That is a workplace issue whether or not the loan is the employee’s own contract. Unplanned absence in the two days after month-end went up. Our fleet manager linked at least three missed Mombasa runs to drivers who were “sorting out” loans. I can’t give you a clean shilling figure for that, and that’s part of the point: those costs don’t sit on the payroll line. They sit on operations, fleet, reception and supervisors’ time.

We reopened in September 2025, but not the old informal scheme. We put it in writing: maximum 40% of net pay, once per pay cycle, repaid in full at the next payroll, no fee, request through the payroll portal rather than my office. We check the Employment Act limit on total deductions — two-thirds of wages — before approving, so nobody ends up with nothing at month end. Since reopening we’ve had about 55–70 requests a month, average around KES 9,000. We’ve recovered in full except for two leavers, with total write-offs of roughly KES 14,000 for the year. I’m not saying that’s nothing. I’m saying it’s visible, capped, and smaller than the cost of the missed runs and the reception time — and unlike the absence and the missed runs, it sits in one place where Finance can see it.

On the SACCO point: ours takes two to three weeks to process and needs guarantors. That is fine for a planned purchase. It is useless for a child sent home from school over fees on a Tuesday. At KES 28,000 a month, there is no emergency affordability. The real choice for many staff is not advance versus no borrowing; it’s advance versus loan app. And the loan app does not stay out of the workplace. We had a loader at Changamwe who came to me with six apps running at once, borrowing from one to pay another. It took four months with payroll to unwind. That is what you get when the only remaining option is the most expensive one.

You said the mobile apps are the employee’s own decision and their own contract. I agree with the contract part. But the collection call comes to the supervisor, the absence lands on the shift, and the missed run lands on the customer. The employee’s private decision becomes our operational problem. That’s not a moral argument; it’s a cost argument.

You also said HR becomes the lender of first resort. In our old scheme, yes. That’s exactly why we changed the route. No one comes to my office, no supervisor discretion, no cash. The request goes through the payroll portal, payroll checks the cap and the legal deduction limit, and it is repaid at the next payroll. It is a payroll process with a ceiling, not an HR favour. Our Finance Manager, who originally pushed to close the scheme, now defends it in management meetings because the forecast impact is known in advance. A capped scheme is a fixed ceiling. The old one was a surprise. Closing it doesn’t make the need disappear; it moves the cost to places Finance doesn’t measure.

Brenda, for the 18th, I’d go in with something like this as the shape of a policy you can propose — not as a defence of the old informal scheme, but as a replacement for it:

- **Cap:** maximum 40% of net pay, and always check total deductions against the two-thirds statutory limit before approving.
- **Frequency:** once per pay cycle, one outstanding advance at a time, no rollover.
- **Repayment:** full at the next payroll, no fee or interest, and no new advance until the previous one is cleared.
- **Approval route:** written policy, request through the payroll portal, fixed cut-off date, payroll verifies the cap and deductions. No cash from the HR office and no supervisor discretion beyond confirming the roster or attendance.
- **Reporting:** a monthly one-pager to Finance — number of requests, value, average, write-offs. That gives them the forecast.
- **Support:** keep the financial literacy and SACCO partnership, but treat them as supplements, not substitutes. They don’t solve a Tuesday emergency.
- **Review:** six months, with both columns on the table — advance administration and write-offs on one side; absence, missed runs, reception and supervisor time on the other.

That last point is the one I’d push hardest. If Finance only counts the advance line, the answer is predetermined. Ask them to count the other line too. In our case, the advance line was about KES 14,000 in write-offs for the year. The other line was 61 collection calls, increased post-month-end absence, at least three missed Mombasa runs, and a four-month cleanup on one loader’s six loan apps. Those costs are spread across departments, which is exactly why they get missed.

Peter, I’d genuinely want someone with your payroll discipline in that meeting, because a scheme like this needs someone who thinks about recovery and controls. I just think the answer is a tighter scheme with written rules and limits, not no scheme at all. We tried no scheme. The need didn’t go away; it went to the loan apps, and then it came back through the front door.

— Wanjiru_K
